title: Six of 40 North Pacific model runs had no density 26.5 outcrop in the mean winter map but had open winters in 1985-2014
abstract: We tested whether a zero winter outcrop in a mean map means that all winters are closed. We used verified annual and mean-map aggregates from 40 CMIP6 historical runs. For open-ocean area at or above sigma0 26.5 in 1985-2014, 16 runs had zero area in the mean map, but only 10 had zero area in all 30 winters. Five of the six changed runs exceeded 100,000 square kilometres in at least one winter. Among 24 runs with positive mean-map area, the median ratio of mean annual area to mean-map area was 1.81. The oxygen relation off California remained: rank correlation was +0.74 with mean-map area and +0.70 with mean annual area in 10 runs. In seven runs with large baseline outcrops, the annual band-area ratio for 2005-2014 versus 1965-1984 was 0.77-0.94; their small historical loss remained. These results show that zero area in a mean winter map cannot establish persistent surface closure. They do not measure subduction or show that annual openings renew the interior. We did not compute annual future maps and cannot revise projected closure dates. Code, hashes, aggregate tables and a figure permit reproduction from the cited baseline bundle.

display.caption: Annual processing changes six zero-area classifications in 40 CMIP6 runs in 1985-2014. Interior oxygen links remain. Intervals in panel B use five-year circular blocks. Surface area does not measure renewal volume.

citations.reason: We audit the temporal operators in its published annual and mean-map areas and retain its 40 accepted runs and interior properties. A zero mean map does not establish zero annual surface contact.
Its mean-field future zero-outcrop counts motivate the distinction between mean-state closure and closure in all winters. We do not recompute those projections.
Mecking and Drushka link annual maximum upstream outcrop area with downstream oxygen. We test the meaning of temporal aggregation in a model comparison.
